clinicalPearls: Acute pericarditis has four principal diagnostic features: chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, characteristic ECG changes, and pericardial effusion (Harrison 22e p.2078).

Pericarditic chest pain is typically retrosternal/left precordial, often pleuritic, may radiate to the trapezius ridge, and is characteristically intensified by lying supine and relieved by sitting up and leaning forward (Harrison 22e p.2079).

A pericardial friction rub is audible at some point in approximately 85% of patients with acute pericarditis; it may have up to three components per cycle and is best heard at end expiration with the patient upright and leaning forward (Harrison 22e p.2079).

The ECG of acute pericarditis classically evolves through four stages: stage 1 widespread upwardly-concave ST elevation with PR-segment depression, stage 2 normalization of ST, stage 3 T-wave inversion, and stage 4 return to normal (Harrison 22e p.2079).
Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade is hypotension, soft or absent heart sounds, and jugular venous distention with a prominent x descent but an absent y descent (Harrison 22e p.2081).

Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg) is an important clue to tamponade, but also occurs in about one-third of constrictive pericarditis cases and in hypovolemic shock, obstructive airway disease, and pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.2081-2082).

In constrictive pericarditis the rigid thickened pericardium limits ventricular filling only after early diastole (unimpeded in early diastole, then abruptly reduced), whereas in tamponade filling is impeded throughout diastole (Harrison 22e p.2083).

Kussmaul's sign (failure of venous pressure to decline, or a rise, during inspiration) is common in chronic constrictive pericarditis but is also seen in tricuspid stenosis, right ventricular infarction, and restrictive cardiomyopathy; it is negative in cor pulmonale (Harrison 22e p.2083-2084).
A pericardial knock, an early third heart sound at the apex from abrupt cessation of ventricular filling, is often conspicuous in constrictive pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.2083).

Constrictive pericarditis produces an M-shaped atrial pressure contour with prominent x and y descents; the y descent (diminished/absent in tamponade) is the most prominent deflection, and the ventricular pressure pulse shows a 'square root' sign in diastole (Harrison 22e p.2083).

In developing nations a high percentage of chronic constrictive pericarditis is tuberculous, but TB is now an uncommon cause in North America and Western Europe; other causes include prior viral/idiopathic pericarditis, cardiac surgery, mediastinal irradiation, and neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.2083).
harrison.pathophysiology: The pericardium is a double-layered sac (visceral and parietal layers) separated by 15-50 mL of plasma ultrafiltrate; it restrains sudden cardiac chamber dilation and fixes cardiac position. In acute pericarditis, inflammation produces fibrinous or effusive disease. Cardiac tamponade occurs when fluid accumulates in the pericardial space in quantity sufficient to obstruct ventricular inflow, raising intrapericardial pressure and limiting diastolic filling throughout diastole, reducing stroke volume, cardiac output, and arterial pressure. As little as 200 mL can cause tamponade when fluid develops rapidly, versus >2000 mL when it accumulates slowly and the pericardium stretches. In chronic constrictive pericarditis, healing of fibrinous/serofibrinous pericarditis or resorption of effusion produces granulation tissue that contracts into a rigid, sometimes calcified scar encasing the heart; ventricular filling is unimpeded early in diastole then abruptly halts at the pericardium's elastic limit. End-diastolic pressures in both ventricles and mean atrial, pulmonary venous, and systemic venous pressures equalize within ~5 mmHg, while resting systolic function is typically normal or only mildly impaired (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2081, p.2083).
additionalDifferentials: Acute myocardial infarction (common confusion with acute pericarditis; in pericarditis ST elevations are upwardly concave, biomarker elevations are modest, and pain may precede or coincide with fever) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2083)
Restrictive cardiomyopathy (shares restriction of ventricular filling; must be distinguished from constrictive pericarditis because the latter is surgically correctable) (Harrison 22e p.2084)
Right ventricular infarction (may mimic tamponade with hypotension, elevated JVP, slow y descent, occasional paradoxical pulse) (Harrison 22e p.2082)
Cor pulmonale (systemic venous hypertension and paradoxical pulse, but Kussmaul's sign is negative and advanced parenchymal lung disease is apparent) (Harrison 22e p.2084)
Tricuspid stenosis (congestive hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites, venous distention, but characteristic murmur present) (Harrison 22e p.2084)

Hepatic cirrhosis (constrictive pericarditis with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and intractable ascites may be mistaken for cirrhosis; inspection of distended neck veins avoids the error) (Harrison 22e p.2084)
infectionMimics: Viral pericarditis (coxsackievirus A and B, echovirus, influenza, mumps, herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, post-acute COVID, mpox) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2082)

Tuberculous pericarditis (effusion, constriction, or effusive-constrictive disease; suggested by high adenosine deaminase or M. tuberculosis DNA by PCR, often requiring pericardial tissue) (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084)

Pyogenic/purulent bacterial pericarditis (pneumococcus, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Neisseria, Legionella, Chlamydia; from cardiothoracic surgery, lung/pleural extension, esophageal rupture, or valve-ring abscess; fever, chills, septicemia, poor prognosis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083)
Fungal pericarditis (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, aspergillosis, candidiasis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083)
Parasitic/protozoal and syphilitic pericarditis (amebiasis, toxoplasmosis, echinococcosis, trichinosis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083)
nonInfectiousMimics: Uremic and dialysis-associated pericarditis (renal failure; fibrinous, serosanguinous effusions, friction rub common but pain usually mild) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083)
Neoplastic pericarditis (lung and breast carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, leukemia; metastatic invasion, primary tumors, mesothelioma) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083)

Postcardiac injury syndrome (postpericardiotomy, posttraumatic, post-MI Dressler's syndrome; hypersensitivity/autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens 1-4 weeks after injury) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2082)

Collagen vascular / autoimmune disease (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, ankylosing spondylitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, IgG4 disease, rheumatic fever, polyarteritis nodosa) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083)
Drug-induced pericarditis (procainamide, hydralazine, phenytoin, isoniazid, minoxidil, anticoagulants, methysergide) (Harrison 22e p.2078)
Postirradiation (mediastinal radiation) pericarditis, acute or chronic constrictive (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083)
Aortic dissection with leakage into the pericardial sac (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2081)
Acute myocardial infarction and metabolic causes (myxedema, cholesterol pericarditis) (Harrison 22e p.2078)
Familial Mediterranean fever and other autoinflammatory syndromes (Harrison 22e p.2078)
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography: most widely used, sensitive, specific, bedside-capable; localizes and estimates pericardial fluid and shows late-diastolic collapse of the RV free wall and right atrium in tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2082)

Doppler echocardiography: in tamponade and constriction, inspiratory increase in tricuspid/pulmonic flow velocities with decrease in pulmonary venous/mitral/aortic velocities and a leftward septal shift (respirophasic variation) (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084)

CT and MRI: superior for loculated effusions, pericardial thickening, pericardial masses, calcification, and detecting pericardial inflammation; more accurate than echocardiography for confirming or excluding constriction (MRI assesses myocardial involvement) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2084)

ECG: stage 1-4 evolution in acute pericarditis; low QRS voltage and electrical alternans with large effusion/tamponade; low voltage and diffuse T-wave changes with atrial fibrillation in constriction (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2081, p.2083)
Chest radiograph: enlarged cardiac silhouette with a 'water bottle' configuration in large effusion; pericardial calcification (most common in tuberculous constriction) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2084)
Pericardiocentesis with fluid analysis: cell counts, cytology for neoplastic cells, cultures, M. tuberculosis PCR and adenosine deaminase (Harrison 22e p.2082)
Pericardial biopsy (e.g., via limited thoracotomy) when fluid analysis is non-diagnostic, especially for suspected tuberculous or neoplastic disease (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084)
Laboratory: elevated C-reactive protein and white blood cell count in viral/idiopathic pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.2082)
redFlags: Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and unexplained sudden enlargement of the cardiac silhouette; may be rapidly fatal if not recognized and treated promptly (Harrison 22e p.2081)
Reduced QRS amplitude with electrical alternans of P, QRS, or T waves raises suspicion of tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2081)

Predictors of poor prognosis warranting hospitalization in acute pericarditis: fever >38C, subacute onset, large pericardial effusion, immunosuppression, or evidence of tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2080)
Purulent (pyogenic) pericarditis carries a poor prognosis and requires immediate drainage and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.2083)
Without treatment, tuberculous pericardial disease can progress to constriction; constriction should be treated surgically (Harrison 22e p.2084)
harrison.prognosis: Viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis usually runs its course in a few days to 4 weeks; recurrent (relapsing) pericarditis occurs in approximately one-fourth of patients, and both tamponade and constriction are possible but infrequent complications. Most patients with acute pericarditis can be managed as outpatients with careful follow-up. Untreated cardiac tamponade may be rapidly fatal. Purulent pericarditis generally has a poor prognosis. Without treatment, tuberculous pericardial disease may progress to constriction. Pericardial resection is the only definitive treatment of constrictive pericarditis, with benefits accruing progressively over months; operative mortality is in the range of 5-10% even at experienced centers, highest in the most severe disease, especially radiation-induced (Harrison 22e p.2080, p.2082, p.2083, p.2084).
pitfalls: Distinguishing constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy is critical because constriction is surgically correctable; their hemodynamics overlap (square-root sign and equalized diastolic pressures occur in both) and echocardiography alone cannot definitively establish or exclude constriction, so MRI/CT is needed (Harrison 22e p.2083, p.2084).

Acute pericarditis is commonly mistaken for AMI and vice versa; in pericarditis the ST elevations are upwardly concave, reciprocal depression is limited to aVR/V1, and biomarker rises (from epi-myocarditis) are modest relative to AMI (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2083).
Pericardial calcification may occur without constriction, and constriction may occur without calcification, so calcification neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2084).
Acute idiopathic pericarditis is a diagnosis of exclusion with no specific test; all other causes of fibrinous pericarditis must be considered (Harrison 22e p.2082-2083).

Constrictive pericarditis with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and intractable ascites can be misdiagnosed as hepatic cirrhosis unless the distended neck veins with characteristic waveform are recognized (Harrison 22e p.2084).
Pain is often absent in slowly developing tuberculous, postirradiation, neoplastic, and uremic pericarditis, so its absence does not exclude pericardial disease (Harrison 22e p.2079).
Anticoagulants should be avoided in acute pericarditis because they could cause bleeding into the pericardial cavity and tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2080).
harrison.severityClassification: Clinical classification (Table 281-1): I. Acute pericarditis (<6 weeks) - A. Fibrinous, B. Effusive (serous or sanguineous); II. Subacute pericarditis (6 weeks to 6 months) - A. Effusive-constrictive, B. Constrictive; III. Chronic pericarditis (>6 months) - A. Constrictive, B. Adhesive (nonconstrictive). Etiologic classification: infectious, noninfectious, and presumed autoimmune. Table 281-2 distinguishes tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, right ventricular myocardial infarction, and effusive-constrictive pericarditis by clinical, ECG, echocardiographic, and CT/MRI features (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2080).
